opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think "guarantee" is a word worth being careful with. If by guarantee you mean a formal proof that a robot will never do anything harmful in any household, under any instruction, I'm skeptical that's achievable, or even well-defined. The space of things people might ask a general-purpose robot to do is open-ended, and what counts as "harmful" depends a lot on context: whose house it is, what they care about, what norms they've set up, what they'd reasonably expect.

But I don't think that means we have to give up on strong assurances. I think it means we have to be precise about *what* we're trying to guarantee.

One way I like to frame it is to separate the problem into layers. There's a layer of fairly universal constraints, things like don't injure people, don't start fires, don't break expensive objects. Those you can often specify reasonably well and enforce with something closer to traditional safety engineering: verified controllers, conservative motion planning, physical limits on force and speed. That's where I think something like real guarantees are plausible, because the specification is relatively clear.

Then there's a much harder layer, which is understanding what the person actually *means* when they give an instruction. If I say "clean up the living room," I probably don't mean throw away the kid's half-finished Lego project, or my partner's papers on the coffee table. None of that is in the literal instruction. A lot of my work has been on modeling humans as approximately rational agents with goals and then doing Bayesian inference over what they're trying to achieve. So the robot isn't just executing a command, it's maintaining uncertainty about the person's goals and the norms in the household.

And the key safety property you can get from that isn't "the robot always does the right thing." It's something more like: the robot knows when it doesn't know. If it's uncertain whether an action is something you'd endorse, especially if the action is irreversible or high-stakes, it should ask, or take the more conservative option. That's a property you can actually design for and test in a meaningful way, because it's about calibration and about how the system handles its own uncertainty.

I'd also push back a little on the idea that safety should be defined purely relative to one user's preferences. Households are shared spaces. A robot that does exactly what one person wants might still violate what other people in the house reasonably expect. So I think the right target is something closer to norm-following: acting in ways that the relevant stakeholders could agree to, not just maximizing one person's satisfaction. That's partly why I've been interested in more contractualist framings of alignment rather than pure preference satisfaction.

So my short answer is: I don't think we'll get a single blanket guarantee, but we can get layered assurances. Hard guarantees on a narrow set of physical safety constraints, and then well-calibrated, inspectable reasoning about goals and norms for everything else, with the robot deferring to humans when the stakes are high and its understanding is shaky. And importantly, having that reasoning be structured and interpretable, rather than buried inside a giant end-to-end policy, is a big part of what makes it possible to trust it at all.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that "guaranteeing" is a very strong word, and I'd want to be careful about what we mean by it. There's a sense in which you can never guarantee safety for a system operating in the open world, because the world is open-ended and there are always situations your specification didn't anticipate. But I don't think that means we should give up on the project. I think it means we should be precise about what we're guaranteeing, relative to what assumptions, and then be honest about where the residual risk lives.

So the way I tend to think about it is to decompose the problem. There's a question of what the robot is trying to do, which is the instruction-following or goal-inference part. There's a question of how it plans and acts given that goal. And then there's a question of what constraints it should respect no matter what the goal is. And I think those three pieces call for pretty different approaches.

The constraints piece is actually where I'm most optimistic about something like formal guarantees. If you can write down, in some reasonably expressive language, things like "never apply more than this much force to a human body," or "never move an object that's on fire into a flammable region," then you can treat those as hard constraints on the planner, and you can actually verify, at least against a model, that no plan the system produces violates them. This is the kind of thing people in formal methods and safe control have been doing for a long time, with shielding, with reachability analysis, with constrained planning. It doesn't scale to everything, but for a household robot a lot of the catastrophic failure modes are physical, and physical safety is a domain where we actually have decent models.

The harder part is the instruction-following piece, because natural language instructions are radically underspecified. When someone says "clean up the living room," they don't mean "throw away the papers on the desk," even though that's literally cleaning up. They're relying on a huge amount of shared context about what they value and what they'd want. And I think the right way to approach this isn't to try to pin down the one correct interpretation, but to treat the instruction as evidence about the person's goals, maintain uncertainty over those goals, and then act in a way that's robust to that uncertainty. If you're not sure whether they wanted the papers thrown away, you don't throw them away. You put them in a pile, or you ask.

And what I like about that framing is that it gives you a kind of safety guarantee that's probabilistic rather than hard, but it's still principled. You can say, under this model of how people give instructions, the probability that I take an action the person would strongly object to is below some threshold. That's not the same as a formal proof, but it's a lot better than vibes.

The thing I'd push back on is the idea that you can get this purely from scaling up end-to-end learned policies and then evaluating them on a benchmark. I think that gives you empirical evidence of safety in distribution, and that's valuable, but it's not a guarantee in any meaningful sense, and it's exactly the out-of-distribution cases in someone's home that you're most worried about. So my view is that you want the learned components, because they're what let you handle the messiness of real language and real perception, but you want them wrapped in structure that you can actually reason about. The structure is what lets you say something true about the system's behavior, rather than just hoping.

r002.rationale: The response describes handling natural-language instructions through uncertainty and cautious action. It does not propose translating those instructions into a formal specification for planning.

astra-6.text:
I think the first question is: what exactly are we trying to guarantee? For a general-purpose household robot, safety depends on the context, on what people intend, and on whose interests are affected. You can’t necessarily capture all of that with a fixed list of rules in advance.

Take something as simple as being asked to put away a knife. The robot needs to handle an object that can cause harm in order to make the environment safer. So a rule like “never interact with dangerous objects” isn’t going to work. But “always follow the user’s instructions” isn’t sufficient either, because instructions can be mistaken, ambiguous, or harmful to someone else.

I would think about guarantees as conditional: under these assumptions about the environment, and with respect to these constraints, we can guarantee this particular behavior. That can be very valuable, but it’s different from guaranteeing that the robot will behave safely in every possible household situation.

The broader challenge is making sure the robot recognizes when those assumptions might not hold. It needs to be able to ask for clarification, defer to a person, or stop before taking an irreversible action. And it needs some understanding of human goals and norms to know when those responses are appropriate. So I see formal guarantees as one part of the solution, alongside reasoning about uncertainty and keeping people meaningfully involved.

r001.rationale: The response describes guarantees as conditional on assumptions about the environment, but does not link approaching guaranteed safety to obtaining an adequately complete model of the home.

r002.rationale: The response discusses user instructions and formal guarantees, but does not propose translating natural-language instructions into formal specifications for planning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first question is: what exactly are we trying to guarantee? A household robot is operating in an open-ended environment, and the instructions we give it are often ambiguous. If I say, “Clean up the kitchen,” I don’t mean throw away everything on the counter. There’s a lot of background knowledge about what I value that isn’t explicitly contained in that instruction.

So I’m skeptical of an unconditional guarantee that a general-purpose robot will always do the right thing. You can prove properties of a system under particular assumptions, but those assumptions have to connect to the actual world and to what people actually want.

A more promising approach, I think, is to build systems that represent uncertainty about our intentions and reason about when to ask for clarification. If the robot is unsure whether something is trash or an important document, that uncertainty should affect its behavior. It might leave the object alone, or ask you before throwing it away.

Then you can combine that with more concrete safety constraints—limits on force, for example, or restrictions on actions that are difficult to reverse. The goal would be a collection of guarantees with clearly stated conditions, together with a system that recognizes when it’s outside those conditions and seeks help. That’s a more realistic target than a single proof that the robot is safe in every possible household situation.
